title: Brains in a Dish: Stem Cells and Organoids

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What makes a piece of stem-cell-derived tissue an organoid?
cards.back: It arranges itself at least partly like an organ while growing in a dish.
cards.quote: An organoid is a small piece of tissue, grown in a dish from stem cells, that arranges itself at least partly like an organ.

cards.front: A stem cell that can give rise to every cell type of the body is {{c1::pluripotent}}.
cards.back: The brain organoids in this lesson start from pluripotent stem cells.
cards.quote: pluripotent stem cells, cells that can give rise to every cell type of the body

cards.front: What is the four-step sequence in the original human cerebral organoid recipe?
cards.back: Aggregate pluripotent cells into embryoid bodies; steer toward neural tissue; embed in Matrigel droplets; transfer to a spinning bioreactor.
cards.quote: The droplets move to a spinning bioreactor, where moving medium improves the supply of oxygen and nutrients.

cards.front: Why should self-organizing tissue in a dish be tested especially carefully for processes that need its surroundings?
cards.back: Cells retain their developmental program, but the dish lacks most embryonic surroundings. Processes needing outside support may fail even when the cellular program remains.
cards.why: Culture can also add stress, so the rule guides predictions; measurements must establish fidelity even for self-organized features.
cards.quote: The cells bring the program; the embryo brings the surroundings. An organoid keeps the program and loses most of the surroundings.

cards.front: A new cerebral organoid protocol produces polarized progenitor zones. Does that result establish that the protocol recreates mature cortical architecture, and why?
cards.back: No. Self-organized progenitor zones can form while layering remains partial. The program-versus-surroundings rule predicts feature-specific fidelity; mature architecture needs its own benchmark.
cards.quote: Cortical layering is at best partial, and standard organoids have no blood vessels.

cards.front: An enucleated frog egg given a tadpole gut-cell nucleus develops into a normal feeding tadpole. What does that success establish about the donor nucleus?
cards.back: It retained the instructions for a whole animal despite specialization. Success argues against necessary loss of unused genes, although the original experiment left donor-cell identity uncertain.
cards.quote: One clean success answers the question: the gut-cell nucleus still held the instructions for a whole animal.

cards.front: Proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on or off are {{c1::transcription factors}}.
cards.back: Changing which genes are active can change cell identity.
cards.quote: Transcription factors, proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on or off, are the obvious first guess, because a cell's identity is set by which genes are on.

cards.front: Which four factors produced the original induced pluripotent stem cells from mouse fibroblasts?
cards.back: Oct3/4 (Oct4), Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc.
cards.quote: four remained: Oct3/4 (also called Oct4), Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc.

cards.front: A mixture of candidate transcription factors produces stem-cell-like colonies. Removing factor A eliminates colonies; removing factor B does not. What does this test establish about A and B?
cards.back: A is required under the tested conditions; B is dispensable in that mixture. The omission test does not establish that A alone is sufficient to reprogram cells.
cards.quote: Leaving out one factor at a time showed which ones the colonies needed,

cards.front: Why do organoids made from an adult donor's reprogrammed skin cells generally model early development rather than that donor's adult brain?
cards.back: Reprogramming resets many age marks, and neural differentiation restarts from pluripotency. Some source-tissue memory can remain.
cards.quote: The cells then go through neural differentiation from a pluripotent start, which is why organoids model early development, not the patient's adult brain.

cards.front: Two independently reprogrammed stem-cell clones come from the same patient. Must their genomes be identical, and why?
cards.back: No. Both carry the donor’s genetic background, but new mutations can arise during reprogramming and culture, so each clone needs checking.
cards.quote: The mutation comes with the rest of that person's genetic background, plus any new mutations the line picks up during reprogramming and culture.

cards.front: In cortex-like organoid regions, radial glia line a cavity in the {{c1::ventricular zone}}.
cards.back: Intermediate progenitors sit beyond them, and early neurons further out.
cards.quote: Radial glia, the progenitors of the cortex, line the cavity in a layer called the ventricular zone.
cards.section: What the cells build on their own

cards.front: What is interkinetic nuclear migration in the radial glia of a cerebral organoid?
cards.back: Movement of their nuclei toward and away from the apical surface as the cells cycle.
cards.quote: Their nuclei move toward the apical surface and away again as the cells cycle, a shuttle called interkinetic nuclear migration.
cards.section: What the cells build on their own

cards.front: What morphology identifies outer-radial-glia-like cells in cerebral organoids?
cards.back: Dividing cells away from the apical surface, with a basal process and no apical process.
cards.quote: dividing cells away from the apical surface, with a basal process and no apical one.
cards.section: What the cells build on their own

cards.front: On what broad timescale do human cerebral organoids develop?
cards.back: Months rather than weeks; timing varies with protocol and cell type.
cards.quote: Human organoids develop over months rather than weeks.
cards.section: What the cells build on their own

cards.front: Why can cells at the center of a large, avascular tissue organoid die despite oxygenated medium outside?
cards.back: Oxygen must diffuse inward from the surface and is consumed along the way. Without vessels, the center can run out of oxygen.
cards.quote: Oxygen enters only from the surface, and the cells use it up as it diffuses inward.
cards.section: No blood, so oxygen must diffuse

cards.front: An avascular organoid has an oxygen-starved core, and its surface is already at the medium’s oxygen level. Would faster spinning alone solve the problem, and why?
cards.back: No. Spinning cannot raise surface oxygen above the medium’s level or eliminate the internal diffusion path. Slicing the tissue can shorten that path.
cards.quote: Moving medium keeps the surface close to the oxygen level of the medium, but it cannot push the level higher,
cards.section: No blood, so oxygen must diffuse

cards.front: In the spherical oxygen model, a 4 mm-diameter organoid has an oxygenated shell 0.62 mm thick. What fraction of its volume is oxygen-free? Assume concentric spheres.
cards.back: Outer radius = 4/2 = 2 mm; core radius = 2 − 0.62 = 1.38 mm. Core fraction = (1.38/2)³ = 0.328509, about 33%. This is a model estimate, not a measured survival fraction.
cards.quote: the thickest leaves (1.38/2)³, about 33 percent.

cards.front: In single-cell RNA comparisons with fetal cortex, what does an organoid cluster matching several fetal subtypes about equally indicate?
cards.back: Its identity is blurred at that subtype resolution, even if its broad cell class matches. It does not establish faithful subtype specification.
cards.quote: A cluster that matches several about equally has a blurred identity at that level of detail.
cards.section: Cell by cell against fetal cortex

cards.front: A cell-subtype marker occurs in 1,000 of 5,000 reference cells and 60 of 5,000 cultured cells. Calculate the relative reduction in marker-positive share. Is the marker absent from culture?
cards.back: Reference share = 1,000/5,000 = 20%; culture share = 60/5,000 = 1.2%. Relative reduction = (20 − 1.2)/20 × 100 = 94%. The marker is underrepresented, not absent: 60 cells still express it.
cards.quote: Organoid clusters often correlated about equally with several fetal subtypes, and markers of particular subtypes, such as SATB2 in upper-layer neurons, were much rarer.
cards.section: Cell by cell against fetal cortex

cards.front: Organoid cells show high stress-gene expression and blurred subtype identities. After transplantation into mouse cortex, stress genes fall and some subtype matches improve. Can this separate the effects of blood supply from other host signals?
cards.back: No. The rule identifies missing surroundings as candidates, and transplantation supports an environmental contribution. Because a host changes several surroundings together, the result does not isolate blood supply or any particular signal.
cards.quote: those stress genes fell and some cells came to resemble primary subtypes more closely, which suggests that the culture environment contributes.
cards.section: Cell by cell against fetal cortex

cards.front: Why do most cerebral organoid protocols lack microglia, and what exception prevents assuming they are always absent?
cards.back: Microglia originate in the yolk sac, outside the neural tube. Some unguided organoids form mesoderm and sometimes contain microglia-like cells.
cards.quote: Most protocols lack them, because microglia come from the yolk sac, outside the neural tube.

cards.front: A neural organoid contains local interacting cells but no distant target tissue. Should normal local survival establish that target-dependent developmental neuron survival is reproduced, and why?
cards.back: No. Local partners can affect survival, but the target-dependent process requires competition for limited survival signals from distant targets that this preparation lacks.
cards.quote: neurons are made in excess and compete for limited survival signals from those targets

cards.front: A preparation made by fusing differently patterned brain-region organoids is an {{c1::assembloid}}.
cards.back: Fusion supplies a regional partner missing from a single organoid.
cards.quote: Pașca's group later named such fused preparations assembloids.

cards.front: What developmental event was modeled when labelled ventral forebrain cells entered a fused cortical spheroid in repeated jumps?
cards.back: Tangential interneuron migration from ventral forebrain into cortex. Cells moved saltatorily, with the leading process extending before the nucleus followed.
cards.quote: Most cortical inhibitory interneurons, for example, are born in the ventral forebrain and migrate tangentially into cortex (see tangential migration).

cards.front: In equal tracking intervals, migrating cells make 8 forward jumps of 25 micrometres before a perturbation and 12 jumps of 10 micrometres afterward. Assuming distance = jumps × length, how does distance change?
cards.back: Before: 8 × 25 = 200 micrometres. After: 12 × 10 = 120 micrometres. Distance falls by (200 − 120)/200 × 100 = 40%, despite more jumps; jump count alone misrepresents forward movement.
cards.quote: Patient interneurons made more jumps, but shorter ones, and moved less efficiently overall.

cards.front: Timothy syndrome interneurons migrate inefficiently even when patient ventral spheroids are fused to control cortex. L-type channel blockade improves migration. What do these two interventions support, and what remains unproved?
cards.back: They support an intrinsic contribution to the migration defect and a contribution of L-type channel activity. The program-versus-surroundings rule motivates swapping regional partners; the interventions do not establish that surroundings are irrelevant or explain the whole disorder.
cards.quote: Patient ventral spheroids fused to control cortical spheroids still showed the defect, so it lay at least partly in the interneurons themselves.

cards.front: How do regional fusion and transplantation differ in the missing surroundings they restore to a brain organoid?
cards.back: Fusion supplies another brain region. Transplantation can supply blood and sensory input. Each restores only part of what a single organoid lacks.
cards.quote: Fusion puts back a second region; transplantation puts back blood and sensory input, among others.

cards.front: Human cortical organoids transplanted into newborn rat cortex gain blood supply and respond to whisker deflection. Would these results justify treating the graft as a mature human brain?
cards.back: No. The rule predicts that a host can restore missing blood and input, which these results support. Restoring those surroundings does not establish mature human architecture, timing or function; each feature still needs benchmarking.
cards.quote: Each restores only part of what a single organoid lacks,

cards.front: Organoids from one patient are smaller than organoids from unrelated controls. Does that comparison alone identify the patient’s mutation as the cause, and why?
cards.back: No. Donor genetic background, clone-specific changes and culture batch can also explain the difference. Changing the candidate gene while controlling these alternatives strengthens causal attribution.
cards.quote: Spreading the comparison still leaves the gene only correlated with the result.

cards.front: All patient organoids were grown in one culture batch and all controls in another. Design a comparison that tests whether batch explains their size difference.
cards.back: Grow patient and control lines side by side in the same batches, repeat across batches, and account for batch in the analysis. Otherwise batch and patient status remain confounded.
cards.quote: One person's organoids are small. List three explanations other than the mutation, and one experiment that tests each.

cards.front: A small-organoid phenotype appears in just one reprogrammed patient clone. What replication would test whether it is a quirk of that cell line?
cards.back: Test several independent clones from the same patient and check them for genome changes. Agreement reduces a clone-specific explanation, but shared donor background remains a possible cause.
cards.quote: The mutation comes with the rest of that person's genetic background, plus any new mutations the line picks up during reprogramming and culture.

cards.front: Why is final organoid size alone a weak measure of a mutation’s effect if patient cultures started with more cells than controls?
cards.back: The starting cell numbers differ, so final size mixes initial conditions with later development. Compare starting conditions and measure the proposed cellular mechanism.
cards.quote: patient cells had to be seeded at a higher number to make embryoid bodies of comparable size, so final size alone was a weak readout.

cards.front: Restoring CDK5RAP2 in patient organoids increases radial glia, while reducing its expression in controls shifts cells toward neurons. What mechanism do the opposing interventions support?
cards.back: Loss of CDK5RAP2 promotes early neuron birth at the expense of progenitors. The rescue and reduction support causality for that cellular phenotype.
cards.quote: They reduced the gene's expression in control tissue with two different short hairpin RNAs, which make cells destroy the gene's messenger RNA,

cards.front: Why does obtaining the same phenotype with two different gene-silencing reagents strengthen an experiment?
cards.back: It reduces the chance that a reagent-specific off-target effect explains the phenotype. It strengthens the inference without eliminating every alternative explanation.
cards.quote: Using two different ones lowers the chance that an off-target effect, a hairpin silencing some other gene, explains the result.

cards.front: A mutation is proposed to make progenitors leave the cell cycle early, but patient organoids also began with different cell numbers. Design a test that addresses both causality and the proposed mechanism.
cards.back: Correct the mutation in the patient line or introduce it into a control line; compare matched starting conditions across batches. Pulse with labelled nucleotide, then stain later for early neuronal fate. The rule makes an intracellular progenitor defect plausible; gene intervention and fate measurement must establish it.
cards.quote: A pulse of labelled nucleotide, followed later by staining, shows whether more progenitors leave the cycle and become neurons early.

cards.front: A mutation is proposed to act only in a cell population absent from a tissue model. Mutant and control tissues look identical. What does the negative result show?
cards.back: It does not test the proposed action in the absent cells and cannot clear the mutation. Verify the relevant cell population before interpreting the negative result.
cards.quote: a protocol that makes none cannot test this gene.

cards.front: A candidate mutation associated with cortical malformation is expressed mainly in microglia. How could adding patient or control microglia to patient or control organoids localize a contribution to the phenotype?
cards.back: Cross both microglial sources with both tissue sources, matching added-cell number and state. A defect following patient microglia supports their contribution. The missing-surroundings rule motivates adding them; multiple clones, donors and gene correction still test alternatives, and other missing surroundings limit the conclusion.
cards.quote: If the defect follows the patient microglia whatever the tissue, they contribute to it,

cards.front: Frog nuclear transfer left concern that rare unspecialized donor cells explained success. How does making mice from transferred mature lymphocyte nuclei address that concern?
cards.back: Rearranged antibody or T-cell receptor genes mark the donor as specialized; mice retaining those rearrangements trace success to that donor. The rule being tested is that specialization can preserve the developmental instructions in a nucleus. Marked nuclear transfer addresses donor identity as well as developmental potential.
cards.quote: Those cells have rearranged their antibody or T-cell receptor genes, which marks a donor as fully specialized.

cards.front: Why did survival under the original stem-cell reporter selection not establish that the first induced pluripotent lines were equivalent to embryonic stem cells?
cards.back: The reporter selected activation of part of the stem-cell program. Expression still differed, and the reported tests produced no live chimeric mice.
cards.quote: The first lines were imperfect: their gene expression differed from embryonic stem cells, and in the tests reported they gave no live chimeric mice
cards.section: How good the first iPS cells were

cards.front: Why does coordinated electrical firing in a neural organoid fail to establish that it functions as a whole brain?
cards.back: Local coordinated activity does not establish sensory input, normal long-range connections or mature brain organization. Electrical activity alone cannot validate all those features.
cards.quote: Coordinated firing in tissue with no inputs is a long way from a working brain,

cards.front: What three ethical issues arise when growing increasingly complex brain organoids and transplanting them?
cards.back: Donor consent, welfare of recipient animals, and how complex the tissue should become.
cards.quote: consent from cell donors, the welfare of animals that receive organoid transplants, and how complex such tissue should become.
